title: 22. Interview: Design Facebook News Feed
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Facebook News Feed — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Facebook News Feed interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read**: write gives O(1) reads but O(N) writes per post (lethal for celebs); read gives O(N) reads but O(1) writes. Hybrid (skip celebs on write, pull on read) is the industry-standard compromise Facebook has used for over a decade.
- **TAO (graph store) vs relational schema**: TAO forces graph-shaped queries but scales horizontally to 1 B QPS. A normalized Postgres schema would be simpler but cannot scale. Facebook built TAO exactly because MySQL + Memcached ad-hoc caching had coherence bugs.
- **Cassandra counters vs Postgres counters**: Cassandra counters scale to 50 k/s but losey under contention; Postgres is exact but slow. We pick Cassandra + batched increments (60 s lag, 99.9% accurate).
- **ML ranker latency vs relevance**: a complex deep model gives better relevance but > 500 ms latency. A simple recency sort is fast but boring. We pick a lightweight GBDT with 100 ms timeout and recency fallback.
- **Pre-computed feed vs real-time**: pre-compute (write path) gives instant reads but is stale if a user unfollows someone (post already in cache). Real-time always reflects current follow graph but is slow. We pick pre-computed + filter at read time (hide posts from users you just unfollowed).
- **Push notifications: eager vs batched**: 4 B likes/day → 4 B notifications potential. Eager would spam users. We batch per-user notifications (one digest per 5 min) and apply relevance filtering.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why does Facebook use a hybrid fanout for the feed instead of pure fanout-on-write?
**Answer:** Pure fanout-on-write pushes every new post to every follower's feed cache. For a normal user with 300 friends, that's 300 writes per post — manageable. But a celebrity Page (e.g., Cristiano Ronaldo's page) has 150 M+ followers; one post = 150 M writes. Even at 200 k writes/s, that's 12+ minutes of work — by which time the post is stale and the worker queue is backed up, blocking normal users' posts. Pure fanout-on-read (fetch all followees' recent posts at read time) is O(N) per read for a user following 300 friends — 300 Cassandra reads per feed refresh, ~800 ms latency. The hybrid: pre-compute feeds for normal users (write-path), but skip celebs and fetch their posts at read time. The threshold (~100 k followers) balances write cost against read latency. Real-world: Facebook has used this hybrid since ~2010; Twitter, Instagram, and LinkedIn all use the same pattern with slightly different thresholds.
**Visual:**
```
Normal user (300 friends):
  Post -> fanout-on-write -> 300 Redis LPUSHes -> O(1) read per friend

Celebrity (150M followers):
  Post -> SKIP fanout -> read-time fetch from celeb_recent_posts cache

Hybrid read: merge cached feed + celeb's recent posts -> rank -> serve
```

### Q2. What is TAO, and why did Facebook build it instead of using MySQL directly?
**Answer:** TAO (The Associations and Objects) is Facebook's distributed data store for the social graph. It models data as **objects** (nodes: users, posts, pages) and **associations** (edges: friend, likes, authored-by). It's backed by MySQL (persistent) + Memcached (cache) + a TAO middleware layer that enforces cache coherence. Facebook built TAO because the previous pattern — application code directly reading/writing MySQL + Memcached with ad-hoc cache invalidation — had consistency bugs. A "like" might increment the counter but fail to invalidate the cached "who liked this" list; users would see stale data. TAO centralizes the graph operations: every write goes through TAO, which updates MySQL and invalidates the relevant Memcached entries atomically (from the application's view). It also provides graph-shaped APIs (`object_get`, `assoc_get`, `assoc_add`) that match how the application actually uses data. TAO scales to 1 B+ QPS read across thousands of MySQL shards. Trade-off: TAO forces graph-shaped queries; complex joins across non-graph data still need a separate warehouse.
**Visual:**
```
Application
    |
    v
TAO middleware  (cache coherence + graph API)
    |
    +--> Memcached (hot cache, ~1B QPS served here)
    |
    +--> MySQL shards (64+ shards, persistent)
            |
            +--> Object tables (id, type, data)
            +--> Assoc tables (id1, type, id2, time, data)
```

### Q3. How does Facebook's ranking algorithm work, and how has it evolved from Edgerank?
**Answer:** The original Edgerank (2009–2013) scored each post as `affinity × weight × decay`. Affinity = how often the user interacted with the poster. Weight = post-type weight (photos > videos > status). Decay = exponential time decay (half-life ~ 1 day). It was simple, fast, and explainable. By 2013, Edgerank was insufficient — it couldn't model the nuance of "this user watches videos but skips links," "this user engages with close friends but ignores distant acquaintances." Facebook replaced it with a **multitask machine learning model** that predicts the probability of multiple engagement types (like, comment, share, dwell, click, hide, report) and combines them with weights reflecting business value. The model is a deep neural network (initially GBDT, now deep) trained on billions of historical interactions. Features include: user-poster affinity, post type, post age, post popularity (early engagement), user's recent activity, time of day, device, and hundreds more. The model runs in < 100 ms per feed request. Trade-off: a complex model gives better relevance but adds latency and is harder to debug. Facebook picks the complex model with strict timeouts and recency fallback.
**Visual:**
```
Edgerank (2009):     score = affinity × weight × decay
                      (3 features, hand-tuned)

Modern ranker (2019+):
  candidate posts (~500)
    -> feature extraction (Redis feature store, ~1000 features)
    -> deep NN inference (multitask: P(like), P(comment), P(share), P(dwell))
    -> weighted combination -> score per post
    -> top 20 returned
  Timeout 100ms -> fallback to recency sort
```

### Q4. How does Facebook handle the celebrity post storm (a Page with 100 M followers posts)?
**Answer:** Five defenses. (1) **Hybrid fanout threshold**: celebrities (> 100 k followers) skip the write-path fanout entirely — no worker load. Their posts are pulled at read time. This alone prevents the write-side storm. (2) **Pre-cache celeb recent posts**: for mega-celebs (> 10 M followers), even read-time fanout is heavy — every one of their followers fetching their recent posts at refresh time would hammer Cassandra. Solution: maintain a Redis sorted set `celeb_recent:{page_id}` with the celeb's last 50 posts (1-hour TTL). Feed service reads from Redis instead of Cassandra. (3) **Rate limiting on feed refreshes**: cap a user to 1 feed refresh per 30 s. Bounds the spike. (4) **Circuit breaker**: if Redis or Cassandra hit a latency threshold, the feed service returns cached/stale feed with a banner ("Showing older posts temporarily"). (5) **Pre-warm for known events**: Super Bowl, World Cup, election nights — pre-cache the celeb's posts 1 hour before. Real-world: Facebook handled the 2018 World Cup final (1.1 B people watched) using all of these.
**Visual:**
```
Cristiano Ronaldo (150M followers) posts:
  1. SKIP fanout-on-write (celeb threshold)
  2. Pre-cache last 50 posts in Redis (1h TTL)
  3. Feed service reads celeb posts from Redis, not Cassandra
  4. User feed refresh rate-limited to 1/30s
  5. Circuit breaker -> stale feed on overload
```

### Q5. How does Facebook keep the feed cache coherent when a user unfollows someone?
**Answer:** Pre-computed feeds (fanout-on-write) have a coherence problem: if user A unfollows user B, all of B's posts already in A's cached feed should disappear. Three approaches. (1) **Lazy filtering at read time**: when A's feed is read, the feed service fetches A's current follow set from TAO and filters out posts from unfollowed users. Simple, but adds a TAO read per feed request (mitigated by caching the follow set in Redis with 1-min TTL). (2) **Active invalidation on unfollow**: the unfollow API triggers a worker that scans A's feed cache and removes B's posts. Expensive (500 entries to scan) and slow. (3) **Hybrid**: lazy filtering for normal users (most don't unfollow often); active invalidation for power users. Facebook uses lazy filtering — the follow set is small (~300 entries) and cached, so the filter is fast. Trade-off: a stale post may appear in the feed for up to 1 min (until follow-set cache expires) — acceptable UX. Same approach for "hide" and "snooze" actions: the hidden user's posts are filtered at read time.
**Visual:**
```
User A unfollows B
  |
  +--> TAO: delete assoc (A, follows, B)
  +--> Redis: invalidate follow-set cache for A (1min TTL)
  |
  Next feed read for A:
    1. Fetch cached feed from Redis (still has B's posts)
    2. Fetch current follow-set (B no longer there)
    3. Filter: drop posts where poster not in follow-set
    4. Rank remaining -> serve
```

### Q6. How does Facebook handle push notifications without spamming users?
**Answer:** 4 B likes/day → 4 B potential notifications. Naive push would spam users into disabling notifications (a churn risk). Facebook's strategy. (1) **Batching**: notifications are batched per user — instead of pushing each like immediately, accumulate over a 5-min window and send one digest ("3 friends and 12 others reacted to your post"). (2) **Relevance filtering**: not every notification is sent. A model scores each potential notification by predicted value to the user (will they open the app? will they be annoyed?). Low-score notifications are dropped. (3) **Frequency capping**: each user has a daily notification cap (e.g., 5/day) tuned by engagement data. Once hit, only critical notifications (mentions, DMs) are sent. (4) **Quiet hours**: respect user-configured quiet hours (e.g., 10 PM – 7 AM local); queue notifications for delivery at 7 AM. (5) **Channel preference**: respect per-user channel preference (push vs email vs SMS). (6) **Decay**: if a notification has been queued > 1 hour, drop it (stale news is annoying). The notification service consumes `post-liked`, `post-commented`, `tagged` events from Kafka, applies the above rules, and routes to APNS (iOS) / FCM (Android) / web push. Real-world: Facebook's notification volume is a carefully tuned dial — too many = uninstalls, too few = engagement drop.
**Visual:**
```
Like event -> Kafka -> notification service
                          |
                          +--> batch (5min window): "3 friends reacted"
                          +--> relevance model: drop low-value
                          +--> frequency cap: 5/day per user
                          +--> quiet hours: queue for 7 AM
                          +--> channel preference: push/email/SMS
                          |
                          v
                      APNS / FCM / Web push
```

### Q7. How does Facebook's CDN strategy differ for photos vs videos?
**Answer:** Both use edge caching, but the strategies differ. **Photos**: served as static files from the CDN edge (FOUCS or Akamai). Multiple resolutions are pre-generated (thumbnail, standard, HD) at upload time; the client requests the right one based on screen size. WebP/AVIF format (30–50% smaller than JPEG). 24-h TTL at edge. 80%+ hit ratio. **Videos**: HLS adaptive bitrate streaming. The video is segmented into 10-s chunks at multiple bitrates (240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K). A `master.m3u8` playlist lists available bitrates; the player picks the highest sustainable one and switches mid-stream if bandwidth changes. Each segment is cached independently at the edge — a 1-h video has 360 segments × 5 bitrates = 1 800 cacheable objects. Benefits: (1) only the segments actually watched are fetched (saves bandwidth); (2) segments are small and cache well; (3) mid-stream bitrate switching is seamless. Trade-off: video transcoding is expensive (FFmpeg with hardware acceleration, ~0.5–2× realtime per bitrate). Real-world: Facebook's video pipeline handles billions of views/day; YouTube and Netflix use the same HLS/DASH approach.
**Visual:**
```
Photos:
  upload -> generate thumb/standard/HD -> S3 -> CDN edge (24h TTL)
  client requests best resolution for screen
  80%+ edge hit ratio

Videos:
  upload -> transcode to 5 bitrates -> segment into 10s HLS chunks
  -> master.m3u8 playlist
  client: picks highest sustainable bitrate, switches mid-stream
  each segment cached independently at edge
  1h video = 360 segments × 5 bitrates = 1800 cacheable objects
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A user reports their feed is "stuck" — same posts for 24 hours. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Is the user actually posting/refreshing?** Check the feed service logs for the user_id — are there recent `GET /feed` calls? If not, the user may have the app closed or be on a slow connection. (2) **Is the feed cache populated and fresh?** Check Redis `LLEN feed_cache:{user_id}` — should be ~500+ entries. Check the timestamps of the top 10 entries — if they're all > 24 h old, the fanout worker hasn't been pushing to this user. (3) **Are the user's followees posting?** Check Cassandra `user_posts` for the user's top 10 followees — have any posted in the last 24 h? If yes, the fanout is broken. (4) **Is the follow graph intact?** Check TAO for the user's `follows` associations — if the cache was wiped, the user might appear to follow no one. (5) **Is the ML ranker dropping everything?** Check ranker logs for the user — if the model returns 0 candidates (e.g., a feature bug), the feed would be empty or stale. (6) **Is there a regional issue?** Check if other users in the same data center are affected — a Redis shard may be down. Most likely cause: a fanout worker crashed and missed this user. Fix: replay the last 24 h of `post-created` events for the user's followees to refill the cache.
**Visual:**
```
Stuck feed reported
  |
  +--> Feed service logs: any GET /feed calls? (user active?)
  +--> Redis LLEN feed_cache:{user_id} = ?  Top entries age?
  +--> Followees posting? -> check user_posts in Cassandra
  +--> Follow graph intact? -> check TAO follows
  +--> ML ranker returning 0 candidates? (feature bug?)
  +--> Regional issue? -> check Redis shard health
  Fix: replay 24h of post-created events for user's followees
```

### Q2. The CEO wants to add "Memories" — show posts from this day 1/5/10 years ago. How do you architect it?
**Answer:** "Memories" is a different access pattern: instead of recent posts from followees, we want posts from a specific user (the requester) at a specific historical timestamp. (1) **Storage**: posts are already in Cassandra `user_posts` partitioned by `(user_id, created_at)`. We can range-scan `WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN '2019-06-15' AND '2019-06-16'`. No new schema needed. (2) **Daily pre-computation**: at midnight, a job scans all users with posts on this date N years ago and pre-generates a "Memories" digest. Store in Redis `memories:{user_id}:{date}` with 24-h TTL. (3) **Read path**: app calls `GET /api/v1/memories?date=today` → service fetches from Redis (pre-computed). If miss (rare), fall back to Cassandra range scan. (4) **Notification**: at user's local morning (e.g., 8 AM), push a notification "You have memories from 5 years ago." (5) **Sharing**: user can share a memory as a new post — this re-publishes it through the normal post pipeline. (6) **Privacy**: if the original post was deleted or its privacy changed, the memory must reflect that. Check post's current privacy at read time. Trade-off: pre-computing for 2 B users daily is expensive; do it lazily — only users who open the app get their memories computed. Real-world: Facebook's "On This Day" feature launched in 2015 exactly this way.
**Visual:**
```
Daily job (midnight):
  for each active user:
    scan user_posts WHERE created_at BETWEEN '{N_years_ago}' today
    generate memories digest -> Redis (24h TTL)

Read path:
  GET /memories -> Redis (pre-computed)
                  -> fallback: Cassandra range scan

Morning push:
  8 AM local -> "You have memories" notification
```

### Q3. A new competitor (TikTok) launches and your CEO wants to add "Reels" to Facebook. How do you adapt?
**Answer:** Reels is fundamentally different from the friend-based feed: it's an algorithmic feed of anyone's content ranked by predicted engagement, not social graph. Architectural changes. (1) **Candidate generation**: instead of pulling from followees, the candidate pool is the entire post corpus. Use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) on post embeddings (FAISS / ScaNN) — user embedding × post embedding → top 1 000 candidates. (2) **Ranking**: a deep-learning ranker (two-tower model) scores candidates on watch time, completion rate, replay, share — much richer signals than likes. (3) **Engagement telemetry**: client sends detailed watch-time telemetry (every 100 ms). Stored in a time-series DB (ScyllaDB / InfluxDB) for retraining. (4) **Infinite scroll**: feed is endless, paginated by cursor; pre-fetch next 5 videos. (5) **Video-first**: every Reel is video — requires HLS infra (already have it). (6) **Audio graph**: users tap on a sound to see related Reels — needs a separate `audio` table and `audio_reels` index. (7) **Co-existence**: Reels is a separate tab in the app; doesn't replace the friend feed. Trade-off: Reels cannibalizes engagement from the friend feed; Facebook shows both. Real-world: Facebook launched Reels in 2020 (Instagram) and 2022 (FB main app) exactly this way.
**Visual:**
```
Friend feed:  followees' posts -> rank by affinity
Reels feed:   all posts -> ANN candidate retrieval -> deep ranker

Reels request:
  user embedding (from Redis)
    -> ANN (FAISS) over post embeddings
    -> 1000 candidates
    -> deep ranker (watch time, completion, share)
    -> top 20
    -> pre-fetch next 5 for infinite scroll

Telemetry: client sends watch-time every 100ms -> ScyllaDB -> retrain
```

### Q4. A viral post has 50 M likes in 24 hours and the like counter is wrong. What happened?
**Answer:** Two likely causes. (1) **Cassandra counter drift**: under high concurrency (50 M likes/24 h = 580/s avg, ~5 000/s peak), Cassandra counters can lose increments due to last-write-wins on the same partition. The fix is the batched-increment pipeline (Kafka → Flink → 60 s windows → batched counter update). If the Flink job is lagging or down, counts drift. Check Flink job health and Kafka consumer lag. (2) **Cache staleness**: the post metadata cache in Redis may be serving a stale `like_count` that's not being invalidated. Check the invalidation pipeline — does the batched counter update trigger a Redis invalidate? (3) **Duplicate likes**: if the uniqueness constraint (`post_likes (post_id, user_id)`) is broken, users can like twice, inflating the count. Check for duplicates. (4) **Bot traffic**: 50 M likes in 24 h is suspicious — check for bot signatures (same IP range, repeated user-agents, inhuman cadence). If 30% are bots, the count is artificially high. Fix: deploy bot detection, ensure the Flink batched pipeline is healthy, fix the cache invalidation, and reconcile the exact count nightly from `post_likes`. Display "approximately 50M" (rounded) to avoid precision expectations. Real-world: YouTube shows "1.2M views" with explicit rounding for exactly this reason.
**Visual:**
```
50M likes / 24h
  |
  +--> Cassandra counter drift? -> check Flink batched pipeline
  +--> Cache stale? -> check invalidation pipeline
  +--> Duplicate likes? -> check post_likes uniqueness
  +--> Bot traffic? -> 30% bots? deploy detection
  +--> Reconcile: nightly job computes exact count from post_likes
  +--> Display "approximately 50M" (rounded)
```

### Q5. A user reports they posted 2 hours ago and their friends still don't see it. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Is the post actually published?** Check Cassandra `posts` table for the `post_id` — does it exist? What's the `status` field — `processing` (media still being transcoded) or `published`? If still processing, the transcoder pipeline is the bottleneck. Check Kafka consumer lag for the transcoder. (2) **Did the fanout run?** Check the fanout worker logs for the `post_id` — was the `post-created` event consumed? If not, the Kafka topic may be lagging. (3) **Is the user a celebrity?** If the poster has > 100 k followers, the fanout is intentionally skipped — posts are pulled at read time. In that case, check the `celeb_recent:{poster_id}` Redis cache — is the post there? (4) **Is the post in the feed cache?** Pick one friend, check Redis `feed_cache:{friend_id}` — does the `post_id` appear? If not, the fanout worker missed this friend. (5) **Is the ML ranker dropping it?** Even if the post is in the candidate set, the ranker may score it low (e.g., a bug in feature extraction). Check ranker logs. (6) **Privacy check**: was the post's privacy set to "only me"? If so, friends won't see it by design. Most likely cause: media processing stuck (transcoder lag) or fanout worker crashed mid-batch. Fix: reprocess the media; replay the fanout event.
**Visual:**
```
Post not showing for friends after 2h
  |
  +--> Cassandra: post exists? status=published or processing?
  +--> Transcoder lag? -> check Kafka consumer lag
  +--> Fanout worker: did it consume post-created event?
  +--> User is celeb? -> check celeb_recent Redis cache
  +--> Post in friend's feed cache? -> check Redis LPUSHed?
  +--> Ranker dropping it? -> check ranker logs
  +--> Privacy = "only me"? -> check post privacy field
  Fix: reprocess media + replay fanout
```

### Q6. The Cassandra cluster is at 85% disk and growing fast. How do you reduce storage?
**Answer:** Multi-pronged. (1) **TTL on cached feed entries**: add a 30-day TTL on the `feed` table (cached feeds older than 30 days are never read). Saves 50%+ on the largest table. (2) **Compaction strategy**: switch `posts` from SizeTieredCompactionStrategy to TimeWindowCompactionStrategy — 40% reduction for time-series data. (3) **Compression**: enable LZ4 or Zstandard on tables — 2–4× reduction. (4) **Archive cold posts**: posts with no engagement in 90 days → move to a colder Cassandra keyspace (cheaper nodes, slower reads). (5) **Media offload**: ensure media URLs (not media bytes) are in Cassandra — already done, but audit for accidental inlining. (6) **Likes pruning**: `post_likes` table grows unbounded — keep only the last 1 000 likers per post, archive the rest to S3 (rarely accessed). (7) **Stories**: ensure 24-h TTL is enforced (should auto-expire). (8) **Vnode tuning**: reduce vnodes per node from 256 to 64 for faster repair. Net: 85% → 50% in a week. Real-world: Facebook's migration to TAO + Cassandra was partly motivated by storage cost.
**Visual:**
```
85% disk:
  +--> TTL 30d on feed table (-50%)
  +--> compaction: STCS -> TWCS (-40%)
  +--> compression: LZ4/Zstd (-2 to 4x)
  +--> archive cold posts (>90d no engagement) to cold keyspace
  +--> prune post_likes to last 1000 per post
  +--> enforce stories 24h TTL
  -> 85% -> 50% in 1 week
```

### Q7. The CEO wants the feed to be "chronological again" (no ranking). How do you revert?
**Answer:** Reverting ranking is simpler than implementing it. (1) **Disable ML ranker**: the feed service already fetches candidates in roughly chronological order (post timestamps). Currently it passes them to the ranker; remove that step and return candidates sorted by `post.ts DESC`. (2) **Pre-compute feed in chronological order**: the fanout worker already pushes new posts to the head of the Redis list (LPUSH) — that's already chronological. The cache is already in the right order. (3) **Communicate to users**: announce the change (Facebook tested this in 2018–2022 with the "Most Recent" toggle). (4) **Keep the ranker available as an option**: some users prefer ranked; offer both ("Top Posts" ranked + "Most Recent" chronological). Trade-off: chronological is fair (everyone sees posts in order) but engagement drops 10–20% (ranking optimizes for engagement, not fairness). For creators, chronological means their posts have a short shelf life — a post 4 hours old is invisible. Real-world: Facebook added a "Most Recent" toggle but kept ranked as default; Instagram did the same in 2022. The technical change is a feature flag; the business decision is whether to accept the engagement drop.
**Visual:**
```
Current (ranked):
  Candidates (already chronological from Redis LPUSH)
    -> ML ranker (re-orders by predicted engagement)
    -> top 20

Revert (chronological):
  Candidates (already chronological from Redis LPUSH)
    -> skip ranker
    -> return top 20 by post.ts DESC

No infrastructure change needed — just a feature flag in the feed service.
Business trade-off: 10-20% engagement drop.
```
